bernie-2012.gazette: Carthage, Texas, 1996: an assistant district attorney moved to try a murder case outside the county because too many locals liked the defendant. Linklater put actual townspeople on camera giving their accounts, cut against the dramatization of the same events. The change of venue is part of the court record, not a screenwriter's invention.

the-act-of-killing-2012.gazette: Indonesia's 1965–66 killings were never prosecuted, and the men who carried them out went on living openly in the towns where they had worked. Oppenheimer brought them back to those sites and let them restage what they had done, in whatever genre they preferred. The historical record here is delivered by the perpetrators themselves, on location, unpunished.

breathless-1960.gazette: Coutard carried the camera through actual Paris streets in 1959, working in available light among passersby nobody had hired. Godard handed his actors lines the morning they were shot, and the jump cuts arrived later, in an edit that had to shorten the film without dropping whole scenes. The New Wave's claim to have filmed life as found has been checked against that shooting record ever since.
breathless-1960.prism: Shooting in the street doesn't guarantee honesty; it just moves the staging somewhere harder to see. Half the spontaneity people credit to Breathless was decided at a cutting bench weeks later, and a doctrine got built on top of it anyway.

a-woman-under-the-influence-1974.gazette: No studio would finance it, so Cassavetes and Peter Falk paid for the picture out of their own pockets, borrowing against property to keep the shoot alive. The camera stayed handheld inside a real house, and scenes were allowed to run well past their usable length. When it was finished, Cassavetes distributed it himself, booking theaters and campuses one at a time.

fitzcarraldo-1982.gazette: Herzog refused both the model and the studio hill, so a full-sized steamship was winched over a ridge in the Peruvian rainforest by cable, pulley and crew. Les Blank was filming the production while it happened; Burden of Dreams shows the slope, the machinery and the labor. What the finished film asks an audience to believe was physically done.

a-nos-amours-1983.gazette: Pialat cast an unknown fifteen-year-old, Sandrine Bonnaire, and played the father himself. Scenes were staged loosely enough that the actors often did not know what was coming — the late dinner sequence, with Pialat walking back in, was sprung on the table. The method left a family's collapse looking less performed than overheard.
a-nos-amours-1983.prism: The uncertainty was real for the actors and entirely controlled by the director, which means someone always knew the plan and it was never them. Pialat bought documentary shock with an imbalance the finished film never itemizes.

pauline-at-the-beach-1983.gazette: Rohmer wrote the dialogue down to the comma, then shot it on the Normandy coast with a small crew and whatever light August provided. Critics arguing over the film split along that seam: some heard an exact literary script, others saw holiday footage that happened to be composed. Both descriptions fit the same reels.

the-green-ray-1986.gazette: Marie Rivière was given a situation rather than lines, and the camera followed her through actual August resorts on 16mm, in daylight as it came. Vacationers who wandered into frame stayed in it. The green ray of the title is a real atmospheric event, and the production had to wait on a horizon to get it.

before-sunset-2004.gazette: The film runs about as long as the walk it depicts, Paris afternoon into a Left Bank apartment, with no cut away to anywhere else. Hawke, Delpy and Linklater wrote the dialogue together and shared the credit for it, nine years after the first meeting. Long unbroken takes carried the load, and the clock supplied the structure.
before-sunset-2004.prism: Real time is a promise you can only keep by rehearsing it into the ground, so the loosest-sounding film in the series is the most rigidly built. The nine-year gap did work no script could: the wear on those faces isn't acting.

blue-valentine-2010.gazette: Before shooting, Cianfrance moved Gosling and Williams into a house together on a household budget and had them live the marriage the film would later take apart. The past was shot on film and the present digitally, so the two timelines sit in different textures. Much of what plays as script was found in the room.

boyhood-2014.gazette: Linklater filmed a few days a year from 2002 to 2013 with the same actors, starting without a finished screenplay. Nothing in Mason's growth is prosthetic or recast; the changes on screen are the ones the calendar made. All twelve years were shot on 35mm to keep the image from dating faster than the boy.

vortex-2021.gazette: Noé arrived with an outline instead of a screenplay and let Françoise Lebrun and Dario Argento find the words while the scenes ran. The frame splits in two early and stays split, holding husband and wife in separate images inside one apartment. Decline is shown in duration rather than in summary.
vortex-2021.prism: A split screen guarantees the audience is always missing something, which is roughly the arrangement dementia offers the people living inside it. The improvisation keeps it from sounding like a case study, and it also means nobody on screen ever gets to explain what is happening.

bird-2024.gazette: Arnold shot in North Kent — squats, estates, the estuary edge — with a handheld camera and a lead found through open casting. Scenes were built on location rather than merely set there, with the dialogue left loose enough to move. The social texture is not dressing; it is where the production actually stood.

hard-truths-2024.gazette: Leigh starts without a screenplay: each actor is given a person to build from nothing, then improvises for months before a word is fixed. Marianne Jean-Baptiste returned to that process nearly thirty years after Secrets & Lies. The dialogue in the finished film was found first and written down afterward.

i-was-born-but-1932.gazette: Ozu was still working in silent film in 1932, and he used it for a comedy about two boys who learn that their father bows to another man for a living. The shomin-geki cycle took ordinary salaried households as its subject at the moment those households were losing ground. Japan was already converting to sound; Ozu went on without it for four more years.
i-was-born-but-1932.prism: The boys' problem is that respectability turns out to be a performance they can see straight through, which is close to what the genre was selling the audience that bought the tickets. Ozu films the humiliation and offers no way to unsee it, then sends everyone back to breakfast.
